title: Earning and Creating Value
coreIdea: Money is earned by creating value through your time, skills, ideas, products, and services.
brief: Use your time, your skills, or your ideas to build value and get paid.
lesson: Build value. Get paid. Value can solve a problem, save time, share knowledge, entertain, make something, or help others.

title: Building Income Streams
coreIdea: Learn the difference between earned, business, freelance, investment, rental, creative, and passive income.
brief: Use your time, skills, and ideas to build more than one way to earn.
lesson: An income stream is a way money comes in. Your time, your skills, and your ideas can each create value and earn money.

title: Saving & Paying Yourself First
coreIdea: Save before spending and begin building financial security.
brief: Bring the money you earned into a future payday. Save first, then see how it helps with a surprise.
lesson: Pay Yourself First means SAVE FIRST → SPEND SECOND. An emergency fund helps keep surprises from becoming loans.

title: Budgeting & Smart Spending
coreIdea: Give every dollar a purpose; understand needs, wants, and the 50/30/20 concept.
brief: Give every dollar a job, balance needs and wants, and save toward a goal.
lesson: A budget is a plan for your money. The 50/30/20 rule is a simple guide: 50% needs, 30% wants, and 20% savings and goals.

title: Investing & Growing Your Money
coreIdea: Introduce stocks, bonds, ETFs, real estate, mutual funds, risk, diversification, and long-term investing.
brief: Put money into a mix of investments and give it time to grow.
lesson: Introduce stocks, bonds, ETFs, real estate, mutual funds, risk, diversification, and long-term investing.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Investing can help money grow, but every investment has risk.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: Let’s start early, diversify, and think long term.

decision.prompt: How will you build your first $300 portfolio?

options.label: Mix It Up
options.detail: Spread $300 across stocks, ETFs, and other assets.
options.feedback: You diversified. A mix can reduce the effect of one investment falling.

options.label: Stock Focus
options.detail: Put all $300 into stocks for more possible reward and more risk.
options.feedback: Stocks may rise or fall. A one-type portfolio carries more risk.

options.label: Patient Start
options.detail: Invest $200 in ETFs and bonds, and keep $100 available.
options.feedback: You started small and kept cash ready. Patience is part of long-term investing.

title: Oil, Gas & World Events
coreIdea: Understand how energy, geopolitics, and events around the world can affect prices and household finances.
brief: Respond when a fictional world event changes energy prices and the cost of living.
lesson: Understand how energy, geopolitics, and events around the world can affect prices and household finances.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Why did food and transportation both get more expensive?

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Energy helps move and make things, so higher energy prices can spread.

decision.prompt: Energy prices rise. How will you adjust your monthly plan?

options.label: Use Less Energy
options.detail: Carpool, turn off unused lights, and protect your savings.
options.feedback: Small changes lowered transportation and electricity costs.

options.label: Pause a Want
options.detail: Move $30 from wants to cover food and heating.
options.feedback: You covered the higher needs cost by making a financial tradeoff.

options.label: Change Nothing
options.detail: Keep the old plan even though transportation and food cost more.
options.feedback: The higher cost of living pulled money from savings.

title: Credit, Loans & Smart Borrowing
coreIdea: Understand credit, loans, borrowing costs, and the difference between productive and dangerous debt.
brief: Compare ways to pay and see the long-term cost before borrowing.
lesson: Understand credit, loans, borrowing costs, and the difference between productive and dangerous debt.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: Borrowed money is not free money. It must be paid back.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Let’s compare the total cost, the payment, and the purpose.

decision.prompt: You need a $400 computer for school and paid projects. How will you pay?

options.label: Save, Then Buy
options.detail: Wait and pay $400 without interest.
options.feedback: Waiting avoided debt and interest, but used money you had saved.

options.label: Small Loan
options.detail: Borrow $400 and repay $440 with planned monthly payments.
options.feedback: The useful purchase had a plan, but borrowing added $40 to the total cost.

options.label: Card Minimums
options.detail: Charge $400 and make only small minimum payments.
options.feedback: Small payments stretched the debt out and raised the long-term cost to $520.

title: Entrepreneurship & Starting a Business
coreIdea: Turn skills and ideas into products or services that solve problems for customers.
brief: Find a need, choose an idea, and launch a small business that creates value.
lesson: Turn skills and ideas into products or services that solve problems for customers.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: People nearby need help. That could become a business idea.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: We should research the need and make a plan before we spend.

decision.prompt: Which small business will you start?

options.label: Yard Care
options.detail: Spend $60 on tools and help neighbors with outdoor work.
options.feedback: You found a neighborhood need and built a service around your time.

options.label: Study Help
options.detail: Spend $30 on materials and use your skills to help students.
options.feedback: You turned a useful skill into a low-cost service business.

options.label: Creative Kits
options.detail: Spend $100 to make and sell activity kits from your ideas.
options.feedback: You created a product. Materials cost more, so sales must cover expenses.

title: Investing & Building Wealth
coreIdea: Go deeper into investing, risk/reward, asset classes, and long-term wealth creation.
brief: Review asset classes, balance risk and reward, and improve your portfolio.
lesson: Go deeper into investing, risk/reward, asset classes, and long-term wealth creation.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Building wealth usually takes a plan and time, not one lucky pick.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: Different asset classes can react differently to the same event.

decision.prompt: How will you add $250 to your long-term portfolio?

options.label: Diversified Mix
options.detail: Spread the money across stocks, ETFs, and other assets.
options.feedback: You used several asset classes to balance risk and reward.

options.label: Growth Heavy
options.detail: Choose mostly stocks for more possible growth and bigger price swings.
options.feedback: The portfolio has more growth potential and more short-term risk.

options.label: Steady Step
options.detail: Invest $150 in a broad fund and keep $100 for future choices.
options.feedback: You added to the portfolio while keeping money available. Returns are not guaranteed.

title: Budgeting & Goal Setting
coreIdea: Connect a budget to SMART financial goals and create a plan for reaching them.
brief: Use the 50/30/20 Rule and build a SMART financial goal.
lesson: Connect a budget to SMART financial goals and create a plan for reaching them.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: A budget helps us decide how to spend, save, and give.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: The 50/30/20 Rule is a guide we can adjust for our goals.

decision.prompt: You have $200. Choose a budget for this month.

options.detail: $100 Needs • $60 Wants • $40 Savings & Goals
options.feedback: You used the 50/30/20 Rule to give every dollar a job.

options.label: Goal Sprint
options.detail: $120 Needs • $20 Wants • $60 Savings & Goals
options.feedback: You adjusted the guide to save faster while keeping needs covered.

options.label: More Wants
options.detail: $100 Needs • $80 Wants • $20 Savings & Goals
options.feedback: More wants left less for your goal. A budget makes that tradeoff visible.

title: Stocks & Owning a Piece of a Company
coreIdea: Learn what shares are, why companies sell stock, and how investors can make or lose money.
brief: Research fictional companies, buy shares, and watch stock prices rise or fall with new information.
lesson: Learn what shares are, why companies sell stock, and how investors can make or lose money.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a company. Each piece is called a share.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Companies issue stock to raise money, but a share price can rise or fall after we buy.

decision.prompt: Research the company cards. Which company will receive your $100 investment?

options.label: Neighborhood Foods
options.detail: Buy shares in a grocery company with steady demand, modest growth, and manageable debt.
options.feedback: You bought shares and became a part-owner. Steadier demand can still come with stock-price gains or losses.

options.label: Sunline Energy
options.detail: Buy shares in a growing solar company whose price has made bigger moves.
options.feedback: You chose more possible growth with larger price swings. A promising industry does not guarantee a gain.

options.label: PlayWorks Studio
options.detail: Buy shares in a creative company whose results depend heavily on its next game launch.
options.feedback: You now own shares in a launch-dependent business. Research helps, but the future price remains uncertain.

title: Compound Interest & the Power of Time
coreIdea: See how money can earn money and why starting early can be such a powerful advantage.
brief: Change the starting amount, monthly contribution, simulated rate of return, and years invested to see growth over time.
lesson: See how money can earn money and why starting early can be such a powerful advantage.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Principal is the money we start with. Interest is growth earned on that money.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: With compound interest, earlier interest can earn interest too. Time and steady contributions can make a big difference.

decision.prompt: Set the time machine. Which long-term plan will you begin today?

options.label: Start Small Now
options.detail: $60 principal + $10 monthly • 5% simulated return • 20 years
options.feedback: You invested the principal and first contribution. Starting earlier gives compounding more time, but the simulated rate is not guaranteed.

options.label: Add Consistently
options.detail: $30 principal + $20 monthly • 5% simulated return • 20 years
options.feedback: Regular contributions add new principal for possible growth. Actual returns can be higher, lower, or negative.

options.label: Bigger, But Later
options.detail: $120 principal + $0 monthly • 5% simulated return • 10 years
options.feedback: A larger start helps, but fewer years means less time for interest on interest. The time-machine result is only a projection.

title: Risk, Reward & Diversification
coreIdea: Understand why higher potential returns usually involve risk and why investors diversify.
brief: Build a concentrated or diversified portfolio, then watch a market shock affect each mix differently.
lesson: Understand why higher potential returns usually involve risk and why investors diversify.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: One exciting stock could climb fast, but one problem could also hit our whole portfolio.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Diversification spreads money across investments. It can reduce one-company damage, but it cannot prevent every loss.

decision.prompt: How will you divide $150 before the market-shock test?

options.label: One Big Basket
options.detail: Put $120 in one stock, $15 in an ETF, and $15 in another asset.
options.feedback: Most of the portfolio depends on one company. Concentration raises the effect of that company’s gains or losses.

options.label: Three Equal Baskets
options.detail: Put $50 in stocks, $50 in ETFs, and $50 in other assets.
options.feedback: You spread risk across several investments. Diversification reduces concentration, though the full portfolio can still fall.

options.label: Lower Stock Mix
options.detail: Put $30 in stocks, $60 in ETFs, and $60 in other assets.
options.feedback: You accepted less single-stock exposure and a different balance of risk and potential return.

title: ETFs, Index Funds & Building a Portfolio
coreIdea: Learn how funds can provide ownership in many investments and how to construct a basic portfolio.
brief: Match each fund term, choose an asset allocation, and build a portfolio from investment baskets.
lesson: Learn how funds can provide ownership in many investments and how to construct a basic portfolio.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: An index is a list used to measure a market. An index fund follows an index.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: An ETF is a basket we can trade like a stock. Our asset allocation decides how we divide the whole portfolio.

decision.prompt: Choose an asset allocation for the next $120 in your portfolio.

options.label: Broad Index ETF
options.detail: Put $120 into an ETF that follows a broad fictional company index.
options.feedback: One ETF gave you pieces of many companies. A broad basket supports diversification but can still lose value.

options.label: Mixed Allocation
options.detail: Put $90 in broad ETFs and $30 in other assets.
options.feedback: Your asset allocation uses more than one kind of holding. The mix should connect to the goal, time, and risk.

options.label: One Sector ETF
options.detail: Put $120 into an ETF containing only fictional solar companies.
options.feedback: This ETF holds several companies, but all share one industry risk. More holdings do not always mean broad diversification.

title: The Stock Market & How Markets Work
coreIdea: Understand exchanges, buyers, sellers, prices, market movements, and why stock prices change.
brief: Match bids with offers and watch supply and demand move a fictional market price.
lesson: Understand exchanges, buyers, sellers, prices, market movements, and why stock prices change.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: A bid is what a buyer will pay. An offer is what a seller will accept.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: When they match at an exchange, a trade happens. The latest matched trade becomes the market price.

decision.prompt: The best offer is $48. Which bid will you place in this simulated exchange?

options.label: Bid $48
options.detail: Match the seller’s $48 offer so the trade happens now.
options.feedback: The bid met the offer, so buyers and sellers completed a trade at a $48 market price.

options.label: Bid $45
options.detail: Offer less than the seller will accept and wait for a match.
options.feedback: No seller accepted the $45 bid, so no trade happened. A bid is a request, not a guaranteed purchase.

options.label: Pay the New $50 Offer
options.detail: Accept the higher offer after another buyer increases demand.
options.feedback: More buyer demand helped move the matched market price up. The stock can still move either way next.

title: Reading a Company — Revenue, Profit & Value
coreIdea: Begin thinking like an investor by examining how a company makes money and whether the business is healthy.
brief: Read fictional company reports and compare revenue, expenses, profit, growth, debt, and business models.
lesson: Begin thinking like an investor by examining how a company makes money and whether the business is healthy.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Revenue is money a company brings in. Expenses are its costs. Revenue minus expenses equals profit.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: The highest revenue is not always the strongest company. Growth, debt, the business model, and profit also matter.

decision.prompt: Which fictional company appears strongest after you read the complete report?

options.label: Neighborhood Foods
options.detail: Revenue $1,200 • Expenses $900 • Profit $300 • Growth 8% • Debt $100
options.feedback: You chose steady profit, positive growth, and lower debt. These support the analysis, but they do not guarantee a higher stock price.

options.label: Sunline Energy
options.detail: Revenue $1,600 • Expenses $1,500 • Profit $100 • Growth 18% • Debt $600
options.feedback: Sunline has fast growth and high revenue, but thin profit and high debt add risk. Revenue alone does not show company strength.

options.label: PlayWorks Studio
options.detail: Revenue $900 • Expenses $1,000 • Profit -$100 • Growth -5% • Debt $300
options.feedback: Expenses exceeded revenue, creating a loss. A turnaround is possible, but this report shows greater risk today.

title: Supply, Demand & Why Prices Change
coreIdea: Explore how scarcity, competition, buyers, and sellers influence prices.
brief: Shop as a consumer, then run a booth. Watch supply, demand, competition, and scarcity move prices.
lesson: Explore how scarcity, competition, buyers, and sellers influence prices.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Only three art kits are left, and a crowd wants them. That scarcity may push the price up.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Let’s compare choices as shoppers before we set a fair price at our own booth.

decision.prompt: You need an art kit, but high demand and low supply raised its price from $25 to $45. What do you do as a consumer?

options.label: Choose a $22 substitute
options.detail: Compare quality and buy a similar kit from a competing seller.
options.feedback: Smart comparison. Competition gives buyers alternatives, and substitutes can reduce pressure on a scarce item.

options.label: Wait for restock
options.detail: Keep your money and check again when supply may be higher.
options.feedback: Waiting protects your cash. If supply rises or demand cools, the price may fall, though that outcome is not guaranteed.

options.label: Pay the $45 price
options.detail: Get the scarce kit now because you need it today.
options.feedback: You met an urgent need, but scarcity cost you more. High demand with low supply often puts upward pressure on prices.

title: Inflation & the Changing Value of Money
coreIdea: Understand purchasing power and why $100 today won't necessarily buy the same amount in the future.
brief: Compare the same shopping basket across several years and protect your purchasing power as prices change.
lesson: Understand purchasing power and why $100 today won't necessarily buy the same amount in the future.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: The basket still holds the same food, but it costs more this year. That is a clue about inflation.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: My $100 balance did not shrink, but it buys less. Its purchasing power changed.

decision.prompt: A weekly basket rose from $80 to $92 while your income stayed the same. Which move best prepares your plan?

options.label: Build an earning skill
options.detail: Spend $40 on training that may help you earn $10 more each month.
options.feedback: Growing income can help answer price increases. Training has a cost, and the value depends on using the skill.

options.label: Invest for long-term goals
options.detail: Move $60 from cash into a diversified long-term investment.
options.feedback: Long-term investing may help money grow faster than inflation, but returns can rise or fall and are never guaranteed.

options.label: Keep the old plan
options.detail: Make no change even though the basket costs $12 more each week.
options.feedback: The new cost squeezes your budget. Inflation reduces the real value of money when income and planning do not keep pace.

title: Banks, Interest & How Money Moves
coreIdea: Learn what banks do with deposits, how interest works, and how money moves through the economy.
brief: Move a paycheck through bank accounts, compare interest, and decide whether a loan is worth its total cost.
lesson: Learn what banks do with deposits, how interest works, and how money moves through the economy.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: A deposit moves money into an account. Checking is useful for spending, while savings can earn interest.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Banks may also lend money and charge interest. We should compare what we receive with what we repay.

decision.prompt: You receive $200 in cash. Where will you deposit it?

options.label: $50 checking, $150 savings
options.detail: Keep spending money available and place the rest in an interest-earning savings account.
options.feedback: The split supports spending and saving. Account rates, fees, access, and protections should all be compared.

options.label: All in checking
options.detail: Keep all $200 ready for bills and purchases.
options.feedback: Checking keeps money easy to use, but it may earn little or no interest. Easy access can also make spending tempting.

options.label: Keep all the cash
options.detail: Do not make a bank deposit today.
options.feedback: Cash is immediate, but it cannot earn account interest and can be harder to replace if lost. Banking gives money other ways to move.

title: Credit Scores & Building Strong Credit
coreIdea: Learn what affects credit scores and how financial behavior can strengthen or damage credit.
brief: Guide a live credit-score meter by making payment, balance, and application decisions.
lesson: Learn what affects credit scores and how financial behavior can strengthen or damage credit.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: A credit score is a signal built from borrowing behavior. It is not extra money to spend.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Payment history matters a lot, and using too much available credit can raise risk.

decision.prompt: An $80 card balance is due. What action will you take before the due date?

options.label: Pay $80 on time
options.detail: Pay the full statement balance before the due date.
options.feedback: On-time payment strengthens payment history and lowering the balance reduces credit usage. Actual score changes vary by credit file.

options.label: Pay $20 on time
options.detail: Meet the minimum, but carry most of the balance.
options.feedback: Paying on time protects payment history, but a carried balance can add interest and keep credit usage higher.

options.label: Miss the payment
options.detail: Spend nothing now and let a late charge join the balance.
options.feedback: A missed payment can hurt payment history and add fees. The exact score impact depends on the account and credit report.

title: Debt & Interest — What Borrowing Really Costs
coreIdea: Examine principal, APR, interest accumulation, minimum payments, and debt repayment strategies.
brief: Test payments on a $600 balance, compare payoff strategies, and uncover the total borrowing cost.
lesson: Examine principal, APR, interest accumulation, minimum payments, and debt repayment strategies.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Principal is what was borrowed. Interest is the cost of borrowing, and APR helps show that yearly cost.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: A minimum payment keeps the account moving, but a larger payment can shorten payoff time and reduce total borrowing cost.

decision.prompt: Your card has $600 of principal at 24% APR. The minimum is $25. What payment do you choose this month?

options.label: Pay the $25 minimum
options.detail: Stay current, but reduce the balance slowly after interest.
options.feedback: The minimum keeps the payment current, but interest uses part of it. Slow payoff generally creates a higher total borrowing cost.

options.label: Pay $75
options.detail: Put more toward the balance now.
options.feedback: The same month of interest still applies, but more of the larger payment reduces principal. That can shorten payoff time.

options.label: Pay $25, then charge $60
options.detail: Make the minimum and add a want to the card.
options.feedback: The new purchase is larger than the principal you reduced, so debt grows. Borrowing for wants at a high APR is risky debt.

title: Insurance & Protecting What You Build
coreIdea: Understand how insurance transfers risk and protects income, property, health, and wealth.
brief: Build a protection plan, then respond when a surprise loss tests the choice between insured and uninsured risk.
lesson: Understand how insurance transfers risk and protects income, property, health, and wealth.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Insurance transfers some financial risk. We pay a premium, and covered claims still may have a deductible.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: The right protection depends on what could be lost, who depends on us, the policy rules, and what we can afford.

decision.prompt: You rent an apartment and drive to work. Which monthly protection plan will you choose?

options.label: Auto + renters coverage
options.detail: Pay $45 for two policies after checking limits, exclusions, and deductibles.
options.feedback: This plan protects two major risks, within policy terms. A premium buys coverage, but claims may still require a deductible.

options.label: Auto coverage only
options.detail: Pay $28 for required vehicle protection and keep apartment property risk yourself.
options.feedback: The vehicle has protection, but belongings remain exposed. Lower premiums often mean accepting more risk elsewhere.

options.label: Skip both policies
options.detail: Pay no premium and accept the full financial risk.
options.feedback: You save the premium today, but an uninsured loss could be much larger. Auto coverage also may be legally required.

title: Taxes & Your Paycheck
coreIdea: Learn gross vs. net pay, payroll deductions, taxes, Social Security/Medicare, W-2s, and 1099 income.
brief: Read a pay stub and make a plan with the money that actually arrives.
lesson: Learn gross vs. net pay, payroll deductions, taxes, Social Security/Medicare, W-2s, and 1099 income.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Gross is all the pay you earned before anything is taken out.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Payroll deductions come out first. Net is the money that reaches you.

decision.prompt: Your pay stub shows $300 gross, $60 in payroll deductions, and $240 net. Which plan do you choose?

options.label: Plan the $240 net
options.detail: Put $60 in savings and keep $180 in checking.
options.feedback: Smart plan! You used your net pay, so every dollar in the plan is really available.

options.label: Spend all $240
options.detail: Use the full net paycheck now and save nothing.
options.feedback: The plan fits your net pay, but no money remains for a goal or surprise.

options.label: Plan the $300 gross
options.detail: Promise to spend $300 even though only $240 arrives.
options.feedback: Gross is not take-home money. Planning with it created a $60 shortage.

title: Starting a Business — Problem to Opportunity
coreIdea: Move from Problem → Solution → Customer → Revenue → Profit and design a small business concept.
brief: Spot a real problem and build a useful solution for a customer.
lesson: Move from Problem → Solution → Customer → Revenue → Profit and design a small business concept.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: A strong business begins with a problem that people truly want solved.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: A solution helps a customer. Their payment creates revenue, and revenue left after costs is profit.

decision.prompt: Busy neighbors need dependable help caring for their dogs. How will you turn the problem into an opportunity?

options.label: Build a booking service
options.detail: Offer scheduled walks and text updates. Customers pay $180 and supplies cost $40.
options.feedback: Problem → solution → customer → revenue → profit. You earned $140 profit after costs.

options.label: Design a logo first
options.detail: Spend $80 on a logo before asking customers what help they need.
options.feedback: A logo can wait. First confirm the problem, solution, and customer.

options.label: Borrow for a shop
options.detail: Take a $1,000 loan for a storefront before making a sale.
options.feedback: The large cost arrived before revenue. Test a small solution with customers first.

title: Pricing, Revenue, Expenses & Profit
coreIdea: Learn how businesses determine prices, generate revenue, pay costs, and calculate profit.
brief: Choose a price that customers accept and that covers every expense.
lesson: Learn how businesses determine prices, generate revenue, pay costs, and calculate profit.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Pricing decides what each customer pays. All the sales together make revenue.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Expenses are business costs. Revenue minus expenses equals profit.

decision.prompt: Each creativity kit costs $6 to make. What price will you choose?

options.label: $14 × 10 customers
options.detail: $140 revenue − $60 expenses = $80 profit.
options.feedback: This price covers expenses, earns profit, and still attracts all 10 customers.

options.label: $7 × 10 customers
options.detail: $70 revenue − $60 expenses = $10 profit.
options.feedback: Customers like the low price, but only $10 remains to grow the business.

options.label: $22 × 4 customers
options.detail: $88 revenue − $24 expenses = $64 profit.
options.feedback: Profit is positive, but six customers walked away. Price affects demand too.

title: Marketing, Customers & Building a Brand
coreIdea: Learn how businesses identify customers, communicate value, market products, and build trust.
brief: Reach the right customers and earn trust with an honest message.
lesson: Learn how businesses identify customers, communicate value, market products, and build trust.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: Marketing helps the right customer discover how your product can help.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Your brand is the promise people remember. Every customer experience shapes it.

decision.prompt: You have $60 to market your creativity kits. Which message will build customer trust?

options.label: Show an honest demo
options.detail: Show families how the kit works and invite customers to share their creations.
options.feedback: The marketing reached likely customers and the honest demonstration strengthened the brand.

options.label: Buy one giant ad
options.detail: Borrow for a $300 ad shown to everyone, even people who do not need the kit.
options.feedback: Many people saw the ad, but weak targeting made the marketing too expensive.

options.label: Make a wild promise
options.detail: Claim the kit can make anyone a famous artist overnight.
options.feedback: The claim brought quick sales, but disappointed customers damaged the brand.

title: Real Estate & Building Wealth Through Property
coreIdea: Introduce homeownership, rental property, mortgages, equity, expenses, cash flow, and appreciation.
brief: Balance a down payment, mortgage, equity, and monthly cash flow.
lesson: Introduce homeownership, rental property, mortgages, equity, expenses, cash flow, and appreciation.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: A down payment is paid first. A mortgage is a loan used to buy real estate.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Equity is the property value you own after loans. Cash flow is rent received minus monthly costs.

decision.prompt: A small rental home costs $120,000 and can bring in $1,200 per month. Which path do you choose?

options.label: Put 20% down
options.detail: Pay $24,000 down, borrow $96,000, and expect $200 monthly cash flow after costs.
options.feedback: Your down payment creates $24,000 in starting equity, and the rent covers monthly costs.

options.label: Put 5% down
options.detail: Pay $6,000 down, borrow $114,000, and expect negative $40 monthly cash flow after costs.
options.feedback: You bought sooner, but the larger mortgage reduced equity and pushed cash flow below zero.

options.label: Keep preparing
options.detail: Save $5,000 more while studying repairs, neighborhoods, and mortgage costs.
options.feedback: You do not own property yet, but a stronger down payment can reduce the future mortgage.

title: Careers, Skills & Increasing Your Income
coreIdea: Connect education and skill development to earning power and career opportunities.
brief: Match your strengths to a career and build skills that can increase income.
lesson: Connect education and skill development to earning power and career opportunities.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Careers grow through useful skills, education, practice, and experience.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: Higher income can take preparation. Compare the training cost with the opportunity it creates.

decision.prompt: You enjoy fixing things and solving puzzles. Which career path will you explore?

options.label: Paid apprenticeship
options.detail: Earn $2,400 monthly while learning from an experienced technician. Tools cost $150.
options.feedback: You gain income and hands-on experience while building valuable skills.

options.label: Earn a certificate
options.detail: Spend $800 from savings, then qualify for work paying $3,000 monthly.
options.feedback: Education costs money now, but the new skill can open a higher-income career path.

options.label: Take the first open job
options.detail: Start immediately at $1,800 monthly without comparing the work to your skills.
options.feedback: You earn sooner, but the job offers less skill growth and lower income.

title: Giving, Generosity & Using Money to Help Others
coreIdea: Explore generosity, charitable giving, community impact, and using wealth with purpose.
brief: Use part of what you built to help people while keeping your financial plan steady.
lesson: Explore generosity, charitable giving, community impact, and using wealth with purpose.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Money can build our future and help someone today.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: Let’s choose an amount that is generous and fits the plan.

decision.prompt: How will you support the neighborhood food drive?

options.label: Give $25
options.detail: A direct gift with room left in your plan.
options.feedback: Your gift stocks meal boxes and your plan stays flexible.

options.label: Unlock a match
options.detail: Give $50; a partner matches the impact.
options.feedback: Your $50 unlocks $100 of community support.

options.label: Give time and $10
options.detail: Help at the drive and cover supplies.
options.feedback: Your time and supplies help the team serve more families.

title: Financial Independence & Designing Your Future
coreIdea: Define what financial freedom means personally and calculate the lifestyle students want to create.
terms: WHAT DOES FINANCIAL FREEDOM MEAN TO YOU?
brief: Design a future lifestyle, then connect housing, transportation, food, travel, family, giving, saving, and investing to the income it needs.
lesson: Define what financial freedom means personally and calculate the lifestyle students want to create.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: Financial freedom is personal. First we need to define the life we want.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: Then we price the plan instead of just wishing for it.

decision.prompt: Choose a future-life plan to model.

options.label: Steady & flexible
options.detail: Moderate housing, reliable transportation, steady saving.
options.feedback: A balanced lifestyle creates room for saving and choices.

options.label: Travel & build
options.detail: More travel plus strong career and investment goals.
options.feedback: The goal costs more, so income and investing must grow too.

options.label: Family & community
options.detail: Plan for family needs, giving, and a stable home.
options.feedback: Your plan includes both personal stability and community impact.

title: Building Your Personal Financial Freedom Plan
coreIdea: Combine income, saving, budgeting, investing, credit, entrepreneurship, and goals into one personal plan.
brief: Turn your campaign decisions into one coordinated personal plan.
lesson: Combine income, saving, budgeting, investing, credit, entrepreneurship, and goals into one personal plan.

dialogue.speaker: maya
dialogue.text: A strong plan connects every money decision instead of treating them separately.

dialogue.speaker: kai
dialogue.text: We should protect the basics, then aim the rest at the future.

decision.prompt: Which foundation will lead your written plan?

options.label: Secure the foundation
options.detail: Strengthen emergency savings, insurance, and debt payments.
options.feedback: Your plan protects today before taking more risk.

options.label: Build long-term growth
options.detail: Direct available money to diversified investments and skills.
options.feedback: Your plan emphasizes future growth with diversification.

options.label: Use a balanced plan
options.detail: Split resources among protection, debt, and investing.
options.feedback: The plan advances several goals without depending on one strategy.

title: The Financial Freedom Challenge — Put It All Together
coreIdea: Final simulation/challenge where students use everything they've learned to make financial decisions and present their strategy.
brief: Manage one final stretch of income, costs, risk, ownership, and purpose. Your earlier financial condition comes with you.
lesson: Final simulation/challenge where students use everything they've learned to make financial decisions and present their strategy.

dialogue.speaker: jordan
dialogue.text: There is no single perfect move. The whole financial system has to work together.

dialogue.speaker: sofia
dialogue.text: Let’s make choices that protect people today and create options tomorrow.

decision.prompt: A strong income month arrives. How will you deploy the surplus?

options.label: Balance all priorities
options.detail: Split money among reserves, debt, investing, and giving.
options.feedback: The surplus improves resilience, ownership, debt, and impact together.

options.label: Prioritize ownership
options.detail: Keep some cash and invest more for long-term growth.
options.feedback: Ownership grows, while a smaller liquid cushion remains available.

options.label: Prioritize security
options.detail: Build reserves and reduce expensive debt first.
options.feedback: Your balance sheet becomes safer before taking more risk.
